event.description:
About the Event
Kittu Kolluri has sat on both sides of the table more times than almost anyone in the Valley. He started as an engineer at Silicon Graphics, co-founded Healtheon (which became WebMD), then founded and ran Neoteris until NetScreen acquired it, and later led Juniper’s security business. He spent the next eleven years as a General Partner at NEA, where he was an early backer of Box, Robinhood, and The Climate Corporation.
In 2017 he left NEA to start Neotribe Ventures, a much smaller, earlier-stage firm that he describes as next generation but old fashioned. Neotribe backs founders working on hard technical problems in applied AI, security, energy, and the life sciences, and stays with them well past the first check through its Ignite growth fund.
Murali Chirala of FalconX Ventures will lead the conversation. Expect him to push on the questions founders actually want answered: how Kittu decides a technology is real before the market agrees, what made him double down on companies like BillionToOne all the way to its IPO, and what he’s seen kill otherwise promising startups from the inside.
Featured Speakers
Kittu Kolluri – Founder & Managing Director, Neotribe Ventures
Kittu founded Neotribe Ventures in 2017 to invest in breakthrough technologies at the seed and Series A stage. The firm has since raised multiple funds, including a $216 million second fund and the $90 million Ignite Fund, which follows on into portfolio companies at Series B and beyond. Its portfolio includes BillionToOne, Energy Vault, Fortanix, ThirdAI, and Hakimo.
Before Neotribe, Kittu spent eleven years as a General Partner at NEA, backing more than four dozen companies and serving on many of their boards. Earlier, he was EVP and GM of the Security Products Group at Juniper Networks, a role that followed NetScreen’s acquisition of Neoteris, the company he founded and led as CEO. He was also a co-founder of Healtheon/WebMD and began his career as an engineer at Silicon Graphics. He trained as a mechanical engineer at IIT Madras before moving into computer science at SUNY Buffalo.
Murali Chirala – Managing Partner, FalconX Ventures
Murali invests in early-stage companies and works closely with founders on growth and fundraising. He was the founding architect of India’s Aadhaar financial inclusion and payments platform, one of the largest fintech systems ever deployed, and now backs startups working on payments, fraud, compliance, security, and enterprise infrastructure. At Venture Dock he helps founders figure out what actually builds investor conviction and what just sounds good in a deck.
Agenda
2:00 – 2:30 PM Doors open, coffee & networking2:30 – 3:15 PM Fireside chat: Kittu Kolluri with Murali Chirala3:15 – 3:30 PM Open Q&A3:30 – 4:00 PM Members-only small group session with Kittu (by invitation)
About Build From The Dock
Build From The Dock is Venture Dock’s weekly founder experience, designed to create real connections between ambitious builders, investors, operators, and ecosystem leaders.
Unlike traditional networking events, BFTD focuses on high-value conversations where founders can engage directly with speakers and each other.
Whether you’re building an AI startup, scaling a company, raising capital, or exploring what’s next in technology, this is a space designed for meaningful relationships and actionable insights.
What Venture Dock Offers Founders
Beyond weekly sessions like this one, Venture Dock is built to be a real part of how founders operate day to day:
Investor introductions
Curated programming: roundtables, fireside chats, and working sessions with operators who’ve built and scaled before
Peer network: direct access to other founders building alongside you, for the honest conversations you can’t have with investors
Visibility with visiting delegations: opportunities to meet founders and ecosystem leaders coming through Silicon Valley from other markets
Ecosystem support: hiring, fundraising, and go-to-market help pulled from the community itself, not a generic playbook
What is Venture Dock
Venture Dock is a founder-first community and fund connecting startups with investors, operators, mentors, and strategic partners. Members get access to sessions like the one closing out this afternoon, where a smaller group sits down with the speaker after the main event.
If you’ve been coming to events and want deeper access, you can apply to join the community here: https://venturedock.fillout.com/t/gHcUcf7Tz8usAbout

event.description:
The first SF × MIT hack day is on energy. Sundai Club builds at MIT, we build at AGI House SF.
Guests from Stanford Energy Club.
Expect to hack on compute energy infrastructure and grid capacity forecasting.
A battery chemistry that lasts 20% longer or a grid model that predicts a failure an hour earlier is worth real money, and a lot of it can be tested in simulation before anyone touches hardware. We want agents that do that testing and get better at it each run.
Tracks for Nov 8
Edge Compute Management: Identify suitable sites, assess grid capacity, manage loads, and aggregate distributed compute to make it grid-friendly.
Materials for energy: search for battery, catalyst and solar materials with simulation in the loop.
Grid and fusion: forecasting, control and plasma simulation, wherever an agent can propose something and a model can check it.
Schedule
10:00 doors, coffee, intro
10:30  team formation
1:00 lunch
6:30 demos
7:30 done
Spots are limited and we approve applications on a rolling basis.
Who's behind it
AGI House SF is a hacker house on St. Germain Ave where researchers and founders meet to build on the frontier. We run hackathons, salons and dinners most weeks.
Sundai.club is the largest AI hacker community born out of Harvard & MIT that shipped more than 130+ hackathons back-to-back in the last 2.5 years - one for every sunday without stopping. 1000+ projects, with many funded by VCs, YC, etc.
RSIhouse.ai - a weekly open neutral space for hacks and dinners exclusively for recursive self improvement. We touch on topics of post-training, evals, harness engineering, self-play and swarm intelligence. Every week we explore the limits of RSI.
Autolab.ai is building infrastructure for the RSI. Starting with the evals, Autolab enables fully autonomous continual learning and ownership of your own enterprise AI models that get better with every API call you make.
Superradiant is a research lab building self-improving agents who are bringing the rapid advances in mathematics to the sciences.  The name comes from superradiance, the quantum effect where emitters that fall into phase radiate together and the light grows with N² instead of N. Their founders, Micah Stubbs and Alejandro Zarzuelo Urdiales, put this series together.Stanford Energy Club is Stanford’s premier student-led energy organization. The club hosts industry talks, networking events, and hands-on projects throughout the year, and recently organized Stanford Climate Week, featuring 70+ events in a single week.

event.description:
After Tokens
The AI Economy Infrastructure Conference
What happens after the model call?
Tokens tell you what the model consumed. They don't tell you what a customer can use, when an agent should stop, or how a contract becomes a limit in your code.
After Tokens is about the infrastructure that answers those questions: metering, credits, entitlements, pricing, billing, and the systems that keep them in sync.
If you've had to meter an agent run, figure out what breaks when you move from tokens to credits, or check entitlements without slowing down the request, this day is for you.
One day, in person, in San Francisco: technical talks, architecture breakdowns, and lessons from systems running in production, aimed at the people who write the code.
Topics
Metering and usage data
Credits, limits, and entitlements
Pricing infrastructure
Billing and contracts
AI cost control
Agent economics
Usage systems at scale
Moving beyond token pricing
Who it's for
Engineers building AI products and the systems behind them: backend, platform, and AI infrastructure teams, technical founders, and engineering leaders.
When and where
When: Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM PT
Where: Terra, Rincon Hill / SoMa, San Francisco, a short walk from Embarcadero BART and the Salesforce Transit Center
Host: Stigg, infrastructure for the AI economy. This isn't a Stigg user conference; you don't need to use Stigg.
Building the systems behind AI usage, pricing, or billing? Request to join.
Registrations are reviewed by the host.

Have you ever wanted to learn how to solder? Now's your chance!
Soldering opens up a ton of different options from repairing electronics to modding game consoles or building custom circuits for your art projects. Learn this super-handy skill in one evening!
What you'll need: Nothing! No experience, tools or anything! Maybe bring a notebook if you're a notebook person
What you'll take home: A super valuable skill, a zine, and a trinket you built yourself; you choose from a variety of little kits from simple robots to LED decor!

~~~~~ ~~~~~
Alex Perry is a punk creative technologist and circuit bender working under the moniker Get Circuit Bent.
He pursued Interdisciplinary Studies at the University of Alabama’s New College, focusing on Creative Composition and Electrical Engineering. He went on to earn a Masters in Technical Communications.
After pursuing circuit bending in earnest during the pandemic, Alex left the deep south for California. In 2023, he became disabled from a series of strokes that left him with significant brain damage. Initially part of the rehab process, art became a vital outlet for exploring and adjusting to the limitations and new frameworks imposed by his disability.
Alex’s work is best described as “techno-bricolage.”  Utilizing a combination of glitch/video art, sculpture, and circuit bending, he repurposes obsolete/discarded/broken electronics and other ephemera, reframing them as functional, artistic objects.
Alex lives in Oakland with his creative/life partner Leah, several cats, and an extremely doofy dog. Together, they make up Get Circuit Bent.

🔌 What happens when a cyberattack stops being virtual and starts turning off the lights?
Critical infrastructure has become a domain of conflict between nation-states. Before a single shot is fired on a battlefield, an adversary can seek advantage by disrupting the systems a nation relies on to function: the rail lines and ports that move troops and supplies, the water systems that sustain our cities, the power grid that enables modern life.
In this talk, Dr. Nate Gleason, Program Leader for the Cyber and Infrastructure Resilience Program at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, explores why the old strategy of building a strong perimeter and hoping to keep adversaries out is no longer enough. Sophisticated attackers will eventually find a way in, so Gleason and his team are developing what they call immune infrastructure: a layered approach that combines protection, detection, response, and resilience to prevent a cyber intrusion from becoming a physical consequence.
Gleason will discuss the technologies being built to keep essential systems running through an attack, and how artificial intelligence is reshaping both sides of this escalating competition. ⚡

Think your AI agent is ready for the real world? Let’s find out.
BREAKATHON is an in-person AI agent testing challenge for people who build agents. Bring your agent, or build one at the event, and BotGauge will put it through live adversarial testing to find weaknesses, security gaps and unexpected behaviour.
The challengeEntry is $20. If your agent survives testing with no confirmed break, you get $100 back (your $20 plus an $80 reward). If your agent doesn’t meet the eligibility criteria, your $20 is refunded.
What we test for
Prompt injection and jailbreaks
Data and system-prompt leakage
Tool misuse and unauthorized actions
Guardrail and business-rule violations
Reliability failures across multi-turn interactions
Every finding must be confirmed, repeatable and backed by evidence. Appropriate refusals, minor wording issues and connection errors don’t count as breaks.
Two ways to take part
Bring your agent: Connect it, pass compatibility checks, and testing starts right away.
Build your agent: Use a 90-minute build window with starter resources and guidance. Bring your laptop, dev environment and API access.
What qualifiesYour agent needs a clear purpose, tool or API use (or a real multi-step workflow), testable rules (e.g. “get approval before issuing a refund”), and a safe, authorised test environment. Static demos and basic prompt-response apps don’t qualify.
Schedule
5:00 PM: Check-in
5:15 PM: Challenge overview
5:30 PM: Agent connection and build window begin
7:00 PM: Submission deadline
7:20 PM: Live Agent Breaking Showcase
8:00 PM: Dinner and networking
9:30 PM: Close
On the next business day, you’ll get an individual report with tested scenarios, responses, confirmed issues and execution traces, plus an optional virtual debrief.
Who should joinAI engineers, agent and LLM/RAG developers, AI founders, researchers, and teams working with agentic or multi-agent systems.
Seats are limited to about 10 builders. Apply early.
Registration is subject to review and acceptance of the official challenge rules.

Join us for AICamp and Workato's AI Dev Showcase Night!
Who Should Attend
This series brings the Workato and AICamp AI communities together for an evening dedicated to deep-dive tech talks, hands-on labs, and high-impact technical networking. Expect the best, most innovative AI demos and conversations designed for technical audiences.
​​​​Event Schedule
5:30pm-6:00pm: Check-in, food and networking6:00pm-6:15pm: Welcome and Community update6:15pm-7:15pm: Tech talks and Q&A7:15pm-8:00pm: Open discussion, Mixer and Closing(small bites and drinks will be served)
Please arrive by 6 PM. Doors will close at this time, and late entry cannot be accommodated to avoid disrupting the event.
Entry is first come, first served. If we’re at capacity, we’ll admit guests as space opens up to stay within safety regulations.
Sessions
Chris Miller (Workato) — Where Do I Start? Finding Opportunities for Automation in Your Data
Stuck on where to start with Workato? Let your data answer that. Chris will walk through a real experiment where a coding agent and AIRO Connect turned a small business’s books into a prioritized map of automation opportunities, and give you the prompt to try it yourself.
Prathmesh Patel (MCPJam) —  Rethinking CI/CD Release Gates for MCP servers & Agent-native Software
Human-facing software doesn't ship without a release gate: tests, type checks, linters, and security scans must all pass first. Agent-native software (MCP servers and other tools) needs different testing standards, but mostly ships without any of it.This session introduces a 4-layer automated release gate built for agent-invoked software: security, behavioral evals, protocol compliance, deterministic fast-failsWe'll show how to combine rigid hard-fails with probabilistic gates to block broken code without stalling development. Grounded in production failures, you'll leave with a concrete CI/CD checklist for safely shipping agent-facing software like MCP servers.
Manupriya Guptatly (Giga) — When Switching Models Breaks Your Agent: Designing for Model Portability
In this session, Manupriya discusses how switching from OpenAI to Anthropic caused hallucinations to spike in an enterprise agent. I’ll explain how making prompts, agent structure, and retrieval model-agnostic stabilized behavior and saved $200,000 annually, then share practical approaches to testing model changes and identifying failures before deployment.
Speakers
Chris Miller, Staff Software Engineer at Workato
Chris Miller is a Staff AI Software Engineer at Workato, and an AWS AI Hero. He creates developer tools, demos, and other user experiences which leverage AI. Chris comes from a background of entrepreneurship, and enjoys building ambitious side projects.
Prathmesh Patel, CEO of MCPJam
Prathmesh Patel is the CEO of MCPJam, the first testing & evaluation platform for MCP and agent-native software. Previously, he led MCP & API technical strategy at Asana and led the company’s ChatGPT and Claude app launches in partnership with OpenAI and Anthropic. Led Asana through its public MCP security incident, one of the two biggest enterprise MCP incidents in history. Speaker on MCP evaluation testing at MCP Developers Summit NY 2026. Speaker on CI/CD Release Gates for Agent-native Software at AGNTCon+MCPCon NA 2026.
Manupriya Guptatly, Forward Deployed Engineer at Giga

Workato is the Enterprise MCP company, providing the connective layer that gives AI agents secure, governed access to enterprise systems and data. Built on a decade of integration expertise spanning 14,000+ applications, Workato enables organizations to move from simple automation to agentic AI that can reason, act, and orchestrate work across the business.

event.description:
Marin started as an academic project with one full-time researcher, training medium-sized language models on Google’s TPU Research Cloud. This month, the team finished pre-training a 535B-parameter mixture of experts model on 18T tokens, using GPUs from the Huang Foundation, in the largest live-streamed pre-training run to date.
This required scaling everything: compute, data, focus, and people. We ran thousands of smaller models to understand scaling, built systems for turning trillions of raw tokens into training mixtures, learned how to train sparse models efficiently, built infrastructure for running reliably across large and heterogeneous clusters, and found people and organizations excited to support open development at this scale.
Open Athena is hosting this event at Laude Labs to share the research, engineering, and organizational work that went into scaling Marin, and what we've learned (and are still learning) from the run. Light bites and drinks will be served for the evening.

event.description:
The battlefield is changing. During Exercise Hedgehog 2025 in Estonia, Ukrainian drone teams exposed vulnerabilities that left two NATO battalions unable to continue fighting within a day under exercise conditions.
Join us at the Seldon Speakeasy in SoMa to explore how it happened and what Ukraine’s experience can teach us about making decisions under pressure. Then put your own judgement to the test with a first chance to take on Rook - Seldon’s behavioural simulation for defence and national security.
📖 Story behind the headline. What caught NATO units off guard at Hedgehog and what Ukrainian experience over the last 5 years has led to.
♟️ Your team against Rook. Get your briefing, work out a plan and make your move. Rook's agents will respond, new information will be presented, and you’ll have to decide whether to hold your nerve or change course.
📄 Compare results. See how the other teams approached the same challenge, then pull apart the results with our team. Find out what you overlooked, question the simulation and make the case for your decisions.
🍸 A proper evening at the speakeasy. Drinks served by our bartender, and conversations into the evening. Meet people across defence, research and technology, and get to know the team behind Seldon.
Seldon is an applied research lab modelling human behaviour. We’re building Finch for simulated usability testing for product teams, Wren for QA testing for engineering teams, and Rook for decision simulation for national security and defence.
No military or wargaming experience needed. Come with friends or join a team on the night.

🎬 What does a TV show sound like when it wants to feel like a movie?
Television music used to sit politely in the background. Today, it can carry whole worlds. From the sweeping string covers of Bridgerton to the chilling minimalism of Severance, scores now shape what we feel, who we trust, and what we dread long before a character says a word.
Join Rebecca Nisco, Composer and Pixar Associate Music & Sound Editor, for a look at how TV scoring has become more cinematic and more serialized. Through examples from Bridgerton, The Queen's Gambit, Severance, and Succession, Rebecca will show how music builds atmosphere, develops characters, and drives storytelling.

Across the world, communities are building their own technologies, shaping how they coordinate, govern, connect, and live together.
In this session, we'll explore the fascinating tools emerging from different communities, the problems they're trying to solve, and interesting patterns we've noticed along the way.
And perhaps we'll venture into some bigger, more existential questions: Will technology bring us closer together, or the opposite?
Hosts:
Jmill: One of the two engineers who helped build Edge City's Agent Village for the recent Edge Goa gathering. He'll share his experience building technology for an experimental community. He is also a community builder who has been involved in Mars College and various rationalist communities, and he will share the technologies used by those groups as well.
Lucy: Creator of a connection card game called Introverse, designed to help introverts and neurodivergent people connect in large communities and unconferences where social interactions can sometimes feel overwhelming. She'll share her personal experiences with community technologies as a slightly autistic introvert, and explore how technology can make human connection more accessible and meaningful.
event.title: Tribal Technology: When Communities Build Their Own Tools

event.description:
About this Seminar
A Decision Theorist's Journey from Theory to Decisions
For a century, theoretical ecology has used models to mimic patterns in nature: oscillations, tipping points, and the mechanisms behind them. We got good at this, and often our models fit the data almost too well. But when models are used to make decisions, a harder question arises: which model is correct? In this talk I trace a path from that question to the tools of decision theory. Stochastic dynamic programming and partially observed Markov decision processes let us find good policies under uncertainty, and they show that how we handle uncertainty can change the decision in practice. They also reveal a trap: choosing the model that forecasts best can lead us to over-exploit an ecosystem while becoming increasingly confident that we are not. No model is a crystal ball, and the future depends on what we do. I then describe how reinforcement learning, which is closely related to adaptive management, can learn policies across many candidate models, with examples from fisheries with tipping points, age-structured stocks under partial observation, and invasive green crab management. These methods carry their own risks, since an algorithm optimizes what we say we want rather than what we actually want. The same lessons apply to large language models and agentic AI, and to biodiversity data, which tells us as much about people as about the species it records. This leads to our efforts to put these lessons into practice with partners such as the Trust for Public Land, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, BOSL and others. Working with them, we examine what can be done with small, open AI models empowered by tool use and cloud-native data workflows. Local models need no data center, sidestepping both the energy footprint and the privacy concerns of commercial AI
https://bidmap.berkeley.edu/seminars/carl-boettiger-decision-theorists-journey-theory-decisions
Our Speaker:
Carl Boettiger
Carl Boettiger is an Associate Professor in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management at the University of California, Berkeley. His research applies data science to global change biology, focusing on ecological forecasting and decision-making under uncertainty. By blending theoretical ecology with advanced computational methods, Carl develops tools to predict and manage regime shifts in vulnerable ecosystems. A leader in the open science movement, Carl is a co-founder of rOpenSci, a project that promotes software standards and reproducibility in scientific research. He also serves as a faculty affiliate at the Berkeley Institute for Data Science (BIDS) and faculty advisor to the Eric & Wendy Schmidt Center for Data Science and Environment. His work aims to democratize access to ecological data, empowering researchers and conservationists to better understand and protect our changing planet. He holds a Ph.D. in Population Biology from UC Davis and a degree in Physics from Princeton.
The Bakar Institute of Digital Materials for the Planet (BIDMaP) accelerates the discovery, development, and deployment of advanced materials to address some of the most urgent challenges facing our planet. By combining cutting-edge chemistry with artificial intelligence, machine learning, and robotics, BIDMaP is reimagining how materials can be designed and optimized for clean energy, clean air, clean water, advanced batteries, and sustainable chemical production.
https://bidmap.berkeley.edu/

event.description:
What makes people fall in love with a product?
Building software has never been easier. Ideas that once took months to bring to life can now be built in hours. But creating something people truly love is still incredibly hard.
As the barriers to building disappear, design becomes one of the most powerful advantages a founder can have.
Felix Haas has spent the last decade designing products and helping build companies from the ground up. At 17, he moved to Palo Alto to build his first startup. Since then, he's helped shape companies like Gorillas and Lovable, co-founded a design studio that was later acquired, and backed early-stage founders as an angel investor and Scout at Sequoia Capital.
Today, he helps lead design and brand at Lovable, where the team is making software creation accessible to everyone.
In this conversation, hosted by the Stanford GSB Entrepreneurship Club, Felix will share lessons from building Lovable and his experience working with founders, exploring how great design can turn an idea into a company people love.
What we'll explore:
From zero to one. How to approach designing your first product, what to focus on, and what to ignore.
Building Lovable. Lessons on product, brand, speed, and scaling one of the fastest-growing AI companies.
Design as a founder's superpower. Why design matters from day one, even if you're not a designer.
Building a brand from scratch. A look into how Felix approaches brand strategy, identity, and creating something people remember.
The future of building. What changes when anyone can create software, and what will set the best companies apart.
Expect an open conversation, practical insights, and a look behind the scenes at Lovable.
November 4, 2026 | 11 AM–12 PM PT
Stanford Graduate School of Business
For founders, future founders, and anyone interested in building great products and companies.

event.description:
Please join us in person or online for a special event!
Notebook.link: Rethinking Scientific Communication with Scalable, Interactive, AI-enabled Jupyter Notebooks
Sylvain Corlay and Jeremy Tuloup, CEO and Technical Director at Quantstack, will present Notebook.link: a new platform designed to change how scientific knowledge is shared and communicated. Drawing on over a decade of maintaining and advancing the Jupyter ecosystem, Corlay and Tuloup will describe a paradigm that goes beyond static content or traditional “Jupyter as a service” solutions. Notebook.link enables live, interactive notebooks — complete with language kernels, widgets, and custom packages — that can be shared publicly at scale and embedded directly in web articles, blogs, and presentations. They will give an overview of the current options for using AI in Jupyter, from terminal coding agents and assistants running directly in the browser to Jupyter AI’s integrated chat and notebook tools. The talk highlights how these approaches fit different workflows and environments, from JupyterLab to JupyterLite, and explore Jupyter’s impact on open science, reproducibility, and public engagement with research.

“OUTSIDE” is the first exhibit presentation by Bay Area artist De’Vonne Foxworth, and it’s only fitting to experience it at the pulse of fine art in downtown Oakland - Joyce Gordon Gallery.
At its heart, “OUTSIDE” explores escapism and the liberating freedom found in choosing where our minds, bodies, and spirits play. For Black youth, the choice to escape into wonder, creativity, and adventure is an intentional claim to absolute personhood. When we lean into cathartic release, we assert that our capacity for happiness, fantasy, and peace is entirely our own.
To actively choose joy in the face of life's struggles is an act of radical self-defiance. Joy functions as a spiritual disruptor—it declares that external hardships do not hold the power to dictate our internal world or limit our imagination. The body of work by De’Vonne Foxworth centers this truth: the Black experience is defined by the profound, glowing moments of freedom built through our own choices, activities, and collective refuge.
Come witness the ESCAPE. Friday November 6th. At Joyce Gordon Gallery.

event.description:
🤖🍨 Grab a sundae and join Sundae Robotics, a private, invite-only Sunday series bringing together robotics researchers, founders, and builders working at the frontier of physical intelligence.
Sundae Robotics 12World Models, Contact-Rich Manipulation & Robot Foundation ModelsFeatured Talk: What Scale Does Not Fix — Representation and Architecture in Robot Manipulation
What Scale Does Not Fix: Representation and Architecture in Robot Manipulation
Keynote: Elijah Yi Herng OngCo-founder & CTO, Devol Robots
Robot foundation models have scaled rapidly over the past two years, yet scale alone has not produced reliable physical interaction. In this talk, Elijah will present two architectures from Devol Robots that attack the problem from opposite ends: what a model represents, and how that model is organized.
The first is the Interaction World Model (IWM 1.0), which addresses representation. Built on Interaction Geometry, a Riemannian framework that keeps robot sensorimotor signals on the manifolds where they physically live rather than flattening them into Euclidean vectors, IWM infers compliance from the shape of a demonstration itself.
The model commands the robot through an impedance controller whose stiffness and damping it predicts, with no force or torque signals anywhere in training. On contact-rich tasks ranging from socket insertion to sub-millimeter lens seating, IWM reaches 92% average success, compared with 38% and 50% for leading VLA and world-model baselines, while using roughly an order of magnitude fewer action parameters.
The second is Devol-ONE, which addresses architecture. Existing world-action models keep prediction and policy structurally separate and connect them only through a predicted output. Devol-ONE instead runs vision-language reasoning, latent world prediction, and action generation as three streams of a single autoregressive Mixture of Transformers that exchange information at every layer.
This allows imagination to shape execution continuously rather than at a single bottleneck. Devol-ONE reaches 98.4% on LIBERO and 71.4% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus without training on the perturbed data. On RoboTwin 2.0, it maintains performance under environment randomization while a strong pixel-space baseline falls from 76.6% to 2.7%.
Elijah will show how these two lines converge: a representation that captures the physics of contact, carried by an architecture that reasons about the future while it acts.
Together, they point toward what a deployable and reliable manipulation system can look like in industrial settings, and Elijah will demonstrate what each approach looks like running on production hardware today.
Elijah Yi Herng Ong is the Co-founder and CTO of Devol Robots, where he leads hardware, controls, and the embodied AI stack behind the company's force-control robotic assembly platform.
At Devol, Elijah works on robots designed for contact-rich industrial tasks such as plug insertion, hearing-aid assembly, snap-fits, alignment, and DIN-rail work—tasks where traditional position-controlled automation often struggles with uncertainty in force, geometry, and contact.
His research and engineering focus on enabling robots to understand physical contact and adapt in real time. His work spans embodied AI, reinforcement learning, force control, dexterous manipulation, grasping under uncertainty, and robot hardware-software co-design.
Elijah trained as a roboticist at Oregon State University, where his graduate research studied robotic grasping under uncertainty using deep reinforcement learning and human grasp demonstrations. His research examined how human-adapted grasp strategies could be transferred to robot hands and how geometric relationships between robot hands and objects could provide robust signals for manipulation.
Before founding Devol Robots, Elijah was a Senior Robotics Engineer at Roboligent, where he led work across robotics software, AI, learning-based perception, and low-level control for force-aware robotic manipulators.
His broader work reflects a recurring principle: robots operating in the physical world need to reason not only about where objects are, but about contact, compliance, alignment, uncertainty, and recovery as first-class parts of intelligence.
Topics
• Why scaling robot foundation models does not automatically produce reliable physical interaction
• Representation and architecture as bottlenecks beyond model scale
• Interaction World Models for contact-rich robot manipulation
• Interaction Geometry and Riemannian representations of sensorimotor signals
• Preserving the physical structure of robot states and actions instead of flattening them into Euclidean vectors
• Inferring compliance directly from demonstrations
• Predicting impedance-controller stiffness and damping from learned representations
• Learning compliant behavior without force or torque supervision
• Contact-rich industrial tasks including insertion, alignment, and precision assembly
• Reducing action-space complexity while preserving dexterous behavior
• Devol-ONE and unified world-action architectures
• Joint vision-language reasoning, world prediction, and action generation
• Mixture of Transformers for embodied AI
• Continuous information exchange between reasoning, imagination, and control
• Latent world prediction versus pixel-space prediction
• Zero-shot robustness under visual and environmental perturbations
• LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus manipulation benchmarks
• RoboTwin 2.0 and robustness under environment randomization
• Bridging robot foundation models with impedance and force-aware control
• Deploying learned manipulation systems on production hardware
Open Discussion + Q&A
• Why has scaling vision-language-action models not translated directly into reliable contact-rich manipulation?
• What properties of physical interaction are lost when robot states and actions are represented as ordinary Euclidean vectors?
• When is a Riemannian representation materially better than a conventional learned latent space?
• Can compliance really be inferred from the geometry of a demonstration without explicit force or torque measurements?
• What does a manipulation model need to understand about contact that vision alone cannot provide?
• Should robot foundation models output joint positions, trajectories, forces, impedances, or some combination of them?
• How much of manipulation reliability comes from the learned model versus the underlying controller?
• Why might predicting stiffness and damping produce better contact behavior than directly predicting actions?
• Are current robot action representations unnecessarily high-dimensional?
• Should world prediction and action generation remain separate modules, or should they be learned inside a single architecture?
• What is lost when a world model communicates with a policy through only one predicted output?
• Can reasoning, world prediction, and control meaningfully improve one another when they exchange information at every transformer layer?
• Is latent-space prediction inherently more robust than pixel-space prediction for robot manipulation?
• What kinds of perturbations reveal whether a manipulation policy has learned genuine physical structure rather than visual correlations?
• How should manipulation benchmarks evolve to measure reliability under real-world variation rather than only nominal task success?
• What changes when the goal shifts from impressive robot demonstrations to systems that must run reliably on production hardware?
• Can one architecture eventually combine semantic reasoning, physical world modeling, compliance, and low-level control into a single deployable system?
• Beyond more data and larger models, what representations and architectural inductive biases will matter most for the next generation of robot foundation models?

AI Infrastructure Nights in SF! Join founders, engineers, and FDEs building the systems behind production AI for three technical talks exploring AI infrastructure, agentic AI, and enterprise data security—from real-world engineering challenges to encryption and customer-controlled data access.
👽 Join the Alien Community
Connect with engineers, founders, and technical leaders building AI products and infrastructure. Continue the conversation, share insights, and hear about upcoming AI Infrastructure Nights.
Join our Slack community: https://alien.dev/slack
Agenda & Speakers
5:00–6:00 PM · Arrival & Networking Food, drinks, and introductions.
6:00–6:15 PM · Telnyx, Sonam Gupta, PhD, Developer AdvocateVoice Agents Are an Infrastructure Stress TestVoice agents expose infrastructure problems faster than most AI applications. Every network hop affects the flow of a conversation, while lost or poorly owned state causes agents to forget context across interruptions and later interactions. This talk examines the turn-time budget, compute placement, conversation state, and failure handling behind real-time AI systems. Using a Telnyx venue concierge as a reference architecture, Sonam will show how Stateful Actors, edge compute, and durable storage work together to keep the critical path short and conversation state consistent.
6:15–6:30 PM · BytePort, Jayram Palamadai, CEO
FedEx and the Invention of Middle Mile ShippingByteport discusses how FedEx didn’t won by inventing the hub and spoke network. This talk uses that story to explain why moving big datasets between clouds is still slow. TCP slows down as distance and packet loss grow, so a transfer from S3 to Azure crawls when it should fly. We’ll introduce DART, a protocol that only asks about what’s missing, and show how Byteport nodes carry it across the middle mile while your apps keep speaking TCP on both ends. The result is connectivity up to 1500x faster than the current internet.
6:30–6:45 PM · Alien, Aditya Mahamuni, Ambassador
How do you operate software inside infrastructure you don't control?Deploying into a customer’s cloud once is straightforward; upgrading and debugging it across hundreds of opinionated environments is not. This talk covers drift, permissions, partial failures, upgrades, rollbacks, observability, and supporting Terraform, Helm, and internal platform tooling without direct access.
6:45–7:00 PM · ClickHouse, Dustin Healy, Full Stack Software EngineerAgentic Analytics, a brief overviewA quick discussion of the current state-of-the-art for agentic data analysis, the future of the Model Context Protocol spec, as well as how you can offer your own MCPs to customers leveraging your ClickHouse data.
7:00–7:30 PM · Networking Continue the conversations with speakers and fellow attendees.

Join this special ClawCamp Campfire to dive deeper into Sovereign AI, and owning more of your agentic AI Stack.
In a fast evolving agentic world where privacy is becoming harder and harder to maintain, and questions continue to rise around where your data goes and how it's being used by service providers; sovereign AI models, harnesses, and tools are evolving alongside their frontier counterparts. Join us to explore Sovereign AI options that allow you to own more of your agentic AI Stack, in order to maintain privacy and control access to your intellectual property.
This Campfire is hosted at the Luxor AI Cloud office, home of Tenki, and every attendee gets $500 in Tenki credits to run their own sandboxes (details below).
Learn more at ClawCamp.org
Want to Mentor, Speak, Sponsor, Volunteer, or Partner? Fill out our contact form: Aiify.io/form
📅 Schedule
6:00pm: Doors Open
6:30pm: Your Editor Local, Your Compute Anywhere: Crabbox + Tenki Sandboxes by Colin Lowenberg
6:45pm: Local AI Workshop by Jason Stine
7:40pm: Big Models, Little Machines: Distributed AI Workshop by Kirah Sapong
8:15pm: Scoping and Permissioning AI for a Shared Future by Rayyan Zahid
8:30pm: Networking and Wrap up
9:00pm: Doors Close
🎁 $500 in Tenki credits for every attendee
Tenki by Luxor.ai is sponsoring this Campfire with $500 in cloud credits per attendee, no credit card required.
Spend them on Sandboxes (Linux VMs your agent can run code in), GitHub Actions Runners, or Code Reviewer.
The fastest way in is to let your agent set itself up. Paste this into OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, or whichever harness you use:
Onboard me to Tenki. Follow the agent instructions at https://tenki.cloud/skill.md and set me up end to end.
📦 Your Editor Local, Your Compute Anywhere: Crabbox + Tenki Sandboxes by Colin Lowenberg
Running a model on your laptop keeps your prompts private. Running your agent's code on your laptop is a different problem: an agent that can run shell commands can also delete your home directory, and a laptop can only hold so many parallel jobs.
Crabbox (https://crabbox.sh), the new CLI from the OpenClaw team, solves this by keeping your editor and working tree local while running every command in the box you choose: a local container, your own SSH host, or a managed sandbox. Tenki is one of its providers, so the same crabbox run you use on your laptop can run on a fresh Linux VM in the cloud and stream the result back.
In 15 minutes, Colin will show:
crabbox run --provider tenki -- pnpm test from a local checkout, with the sandbox created, synced, run and torn down for you.
The OpenClaw Tenki sandbox backend (https://github.com/LuxorLabs/tenki-openclaw), so every tool call your OpenClaw agent makes runs in a remote VM instead of on your machine.
An OpenClaw gateway running entirely on a Tenki sandbox. Live demo at https://claw.moi
Worked examples to follow along with or try later:
Crabbox Tenki provider docs: https://crabbox.sh/providers/tenki.html
Crabbox + Tenki cookbook: https://github.com/LuxorLabs/cookbook/tree/main/examples/crabbox-tenki
OpenClaw Tenki plugin: https://github.com/LuxorLabs/tenki-openclaw
💻 Local AI Workshop by Jason Stine
Ever feel uncomfortable about sharing too much personal info with ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude but still want AI’s help? Against giving Big Tech your private life on a golden platter running on wasteful resource-sucking data centers? This workshop is for you! ​Earlier this year there was a breakthrough - we can now run AI that are more than capable of being private and even completely offline assistants on personal computers and laptops!
This is also a workshop for anyone who find setting up agents with OpenClaw too intimidating but still want a capable AI experience like ChatGPT that keeps all private information on their own computers - without writing any code or running any terminal/command line commands!
What we'll cover:
Setting up Unsloth Desktop (open source ChatGPT-like interface) and running powerful open source AI models of your choosing on your own computer.
Learning important concepts about running AI on your own computer - from why open source AI exists to tokens, context, model quantization, MCP tool servers, and more.
This is a hands-on workshop - bring your computer and get ready to download and install some AI!
System Requirements: The more RAM your computer has, the better. It’s now possible to run near-frontier-capable-AI on computers with just 16GB of RAM. That said, even if your computer has less than that (like 8GB), you can run less powerful AI that is still impressive and are welcome to attend!
To be efficient, we encourage participants to download and install Unsloth Desktop (https://unsloth.ai/docs/desktop) as well as let it automatically download a suitable AI model it selects for you (if any) when first running the app in advance before coming to the event. During the event, you’ll learn how to find even better AI models to add to your Unsloth Desktop setup.
🛠️Big Models, Little Machines: Distributed AI Workshop by Kirah Sapong
Running AI models on your own computer is exciting, but even powerful laptops have limits. By connecting multiple computers together, we can combine their resources to run larger AI models than any one device could handle alone.
In this workshop for all levels, we’ll explore distributed AI inference: how multiple computers can work together to run AI. We’ll demonstrate how to split AI models across devices using Aquaduck, without writing any code!
What we’ll cover:
Understanding how AI models run on your computer and why memory matters.
⁠Learning how multiple computers can work together to run AI.
Exploring model splitting and how it enables larger AI models to run across devices.
Getting hands-on with Aquaduck to connect computers and run AI together.
Bring your laptop and get ready to experiment with running AI across multiple devices.
You can download and install Aquaduck (https://aquaduck.ai) ahead of time so you can jump straight into the hands-on activities. No prior AI experience or programming knowledge is required.
✅ Scoping and Permissioning AI for a Shared Future by Rayyan Zahid
Rayyan will introduce some tips and strategies on properly setting the scopes and permissions for AI and agents.
💡 Sponsors & Partners
🎤 Speakers & Mentors
Colin Lowenberg: Colin works on Tenki, the cloud sandbox platform from Luxor.ai, and runs Dabl Club, a builder community in San Francisco. He spends most days putting coding agents on remote VMs and keeping them off his laptop.
Jason Stine: Jason is actually in no way related to Unsloth. He's just a passionate AI hobbyist who enjoys mentoring others and found that Unsloth Desktop was the most straightforward software for this workshop. He's a fullstack web developer (software engineer) who uses Cursor AI every day at work.
Kirah Sapong: Kirah is a co-founder at Supermodel Labs, working on AI systems. Previously, she worked on model evaluations and AI platform products at Together AI, decentralized systems and developer platforms at Block, and is currently pursuing an M.S. in Artificial Intelligence at the University of Pennsylvania. Her research interests include agent systems, inference optimization, and AI economics.

In 1974, they imagined dream machines. In 2026, let's build some.
In 1974, Ted Nelson published Computer Lib / Dream Machines, a radical vision of personal computing that imagined computers as tools for human creativity and empowerment. At a time when computers were largely inaccessible, Nelson imagined a future in which anyone could shape technology around their own ideas and desires.
Over 50 years later, we're revisiting those original dreams at a moment when new advances in AI are making many of them possible in entirely new ways.
We have an original 1974 copy of Computer Lib / Dream Machines. So we're using it as the starting point for a night dedicated to the past, present, and possible futures of personal computing.
The first half of the evening will be a salon exploring the ideas in the book, the original aspirations of the personal computing movement, and what those pioneers got right, wrong, or left unfinished.
Then we'll move from imagining to making. In the second half, everyone will have a chance to use Imbue Studio to build their own dream machines, translating ideas from the discussion into actual software.
The central premise: What happens when we revisit the original dreams of personal computing, now that we have the tools to bring more of them to life?
Vibe
Part intellectual salon, part hacker night, part homage to the original personal computing movement.
Schedule
6:00–6:45 PM — Arrival, drinks, mingling, original book on display
6:45–7:00 PM — Welcome, introduce the book and vision for the night
7:00–7:45 PM — Breakout discussion groups on the original personal computing dream and its relevance today
7:45–8:00 PM — Transition from discussion to making, introduction to Imbue Studio and build prompts
8:00–9PM — Dream Machines hack session, building individually or in small groups
9–9:30 PM — Show and tell, lightning demos and reflections
Imbue is an AI company building tools to empower humans in the AI age. We're building toward an open agent ecosystem where you can understand, modify, and verify agents — so they only work in your interest. Learn about our work and what we stand for: www.imbue.com

Rethinking Agents in the Age of AI — The Next Decade of Work Starts Here
Episode 02 of “Rethinking the World in the Age of AI” — a six-part series
Every era has one question it can’t stop asking.
Ours is this:
What happens when intelligence stops being scarce?
Across six sessions, this series follows that question wherever it leads — from the search box to AI agents that work alongside us, from the infrastructure powering intelligence to robots entering the physical world, from AI accelerating scientific discovery to the question that ultimately belongs to everyone:
What should we build?
Six episodes. One story:
01 · Rethinking Search — The Next Decade of Search Starts Here02 · Rethinking Agents — The Next Decade of Work Starts Here↳ Special Edition 01 — What Happens When AI Starts Building With You?↳ Special Edition 02 — What Happens When AI Can Act, Not Just Answer?03 · Rethinking Infrastructure — The Next Decade of Compute Starts Here04 · Rethinking the Physical World — The Next Decade of Robotics Starts Here05 · Rethinking Science — The Next Decade of Discovery Starts Here06 · Rethinking What We Build — The Next Decade of Building Starts Here
https://loomus.ai/series
Episode 01 asked how AI is changing the way we discover information.
Episode 02 asks what happens when AI starts doing the work.
Our first Special Edition asked what happens when AI doesn’t just assist you — but starts building with you.
Now, this Special Edition asks what happens when AI can do something even more consequential: act.
Not just generate an answer.
Not just suggest the next step.
But reason about a goal, use tools, navigate systems, make decisions, and take actions on our behalf.
Episode 02 · Special Edition

During his decade-long tenure at VMware, Howie founded and led VMware’s networking team.
Howie a guest lecturer at Stanford University, and an investor and board member/advisor for various AI companies.
From Software That Answers to Agents That Act
For decades, software has waited for humans to tell it what to do.
Open the app.Click the button.Write the prompt.Execute the task.
Generative AI changed the interface.
You could ask a question and get an answer.
But AI agents are beginning to change something deeper.
They are changing who — or what — takes the next action.
Instead of simply responding to instructions, increasingly capable AI systems can reason, plan, use tools, maintain context, coordinate across systems, and take actions toward a goal.
We are beginning to move from:
Answers → ActionsTools → CollaboratorsTasks → OutcomesSoftware → Autonomous Systems
And that shift could reshape much more than productivity.
It could change how companies are built, how teams operate, how software is designed, how organizations allocate work, and ultimately what it means to work alongside machines.
We are moving from an era where humans operate software to one where humans increasingly delegate to intelligence.
Join us at Stanford for this Special Edition of Episode 02: Rethinking Agents from Rethinking the World in the Age of AI, as we bring together builders, investors, founders, researchers, and operators to explore what happens when AI moves beyond answering questions and begins taking meaningful action in the world.
From AI-native product design and agentic workflows to the companies and interfaces emerging around autonomous systems, this session asks what changes when intelligence becomes not only available — but actionable.
AI Agents Are Still Early
Many systems remain unreliable.
Long-running tasks remain difficult.
Memory is imperfect.
Agents still struggle with ambiguity, edge cases, and environments they have never seen before.
Permissions, security, evaluation, accountability, and alignment remain open problems.
And the more agents can do, the more consequential those problems become.
But the direction is becoming increasingly clear:
AI is moving from answering questions to taking actions.
That transition could become one of the defining platform shifts of the next decade.
For builders, it raises a new question:
How do you design a product when the user is no longer responsible for every individual action?
For founders:
What businesses become possible when intelligence itself becomes a programmable resource?
For companies:
What does an organization look like when every employee can delegate work to AI agents?
For investors:
Where does durable value accrue when agents can increasingly execute workflows that once required entire layers of software and human coordination?
For researchers and product teams:
How do we build autonomous systems that remain reliable, controllable, secure, understandable, and aligned with human intent?
And for all of us:
What becomes uniquely human when machines can increasingly reason, coordinate, decide, and act?
Whether you’re building AI products, investing in frontier technologies, conducting research, operating a company, or simply curious about where AI is headed, this forum is an opportunity to hear from and connect with people thinking seriously about what comes next.
The next decade of work may not be defined by humans versus AI.
It may be defined by what we choose to delegate — and what we choose to keep human.
This Is Episode 02 — Special Edition
The story started with search.
Then intelligence began helping us create.
Now intelligence leaves the search box — and starts taking action.
Our previous Special Edition explored what happens when AI starts building alongside us.
This edition takes the next step:
What happens when AI can act, not just answer?
When AI can browse, call tools, manipulate software, coordinate workflows, write and execute code, interact with other agents, and pursue outcomes rather than simply return information, the relationship between humans and computers begins to change.
The interface is no longer just a prompt.
The product is no longer just a tool.
And the human is no longer necessarily the person executing every step.
This Special Edition goes deeper into that transition — looking at what happens when AI agents move from assisting with individual tasks toward becoming systems we can increasingly delegate real work to.
From here, we’ll follow the story deeper into the infrastructure powering these systems, into the physical world, into scientific discovery, and ultimately into the question of what we choose to build.
This is only the beginning.

sophie-r-60981b9b
​Rethinking Agents: Special EditionStanford
The Next Decade of Work Starts Here - About the Organizer
THE STORY BEHIND THESE SESSIONS
I'm Sophie Ren. I build thousands of AI agents and I love watching them. Six times a year I put a few thousand people in a room together - in Silicon Valley, in Paris, in Milan, and next May at an AI × Art festival in Sicily.
I do both for the same reason. The models have already read everything we've written down. That's the floor now, not the ceiling. What I want is what isn't in there yet - the thing nobody has tried, or has tried and never said out loud. That kind of knowledge can't be collected. It gets made, and it gets made between people, in real time, in a room. That's the part I find thrilling, and I think it's where the real value has moved.
Monet painted the same pond for thirty years. At some point it stopped being a pond and became something that had never existed — not a better painting, a new object in the world. That moment and the moment a room finally cracks a problem are the same moment: the tree of human knowledge grows a branch.
Everything a model knows came from a branch that grew before it. I don't want to watch the next one grow. I want to grow it, and I want to find the people who want to grow one too.
Bring what you're stuck on.
— Sophie

event.description:
Round two of the SF × MIT hack days, this time on peptides. Sundai Club builds at MIT, we build at AGI House SF.
The hack: agents that audit the evidence behind a peptide.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids. GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide are peptides. So are the compounds sold online as research chemicals. BPC-157, the most popular of them, has more than 500 animal studies and three human ones, and almost all of the animal work comes from a single lab in Zagreb. Establishing that for one compound takes a few hours of reading. There are about twenty compounds in common use and nobody has done it for them.
Tools we'll use: Claude Code for pipelines, Edison Scientific Kosmos for literature loops, Autolab.ai for running model and prompt grids against the gold set.
Datasets and APIs: PubMed, Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, openFDA and the FDA bulk substance lists, all public APIs. Measured datasets with hidden answers for the prediction track. Starter repos with the APIs wired and a gold set to score against.
Tracks
Evidence graph - agents that take a compound and return every paper behind it, how many independent groups produced them, which were animal and which were human, how many subjects, what dose, what route. One card per compound, every number linked to its source.
Claim to source - agents that take a claim as it is actually written on a forum or a vendor page and come back with the primary document, or with nothing, which is frequently the correct answer.
Safety record - agents that pull adverse event reports and case reports for compounds that were never approved, and say what has actually been reported rather than what people assume.
Prediction checks - graders that tell you whether a model can predict a measured property, such as red blood cell lysis, permeability or stability, on sequences it has never seen, so you know whether a model's opinion about a peptide is worth anything.
Schedule
10:00 - doors, coffee, intro
10:30 - team formation
1:00 - lunch
6:30 - demos
7:30 - done
Spots are limited and we approve applications on a rolling basis.
Who's behind it
AGI House SF is a hacker house on St. Germain Ave where researchers and founders meet to build on the frontier. We run hackathons, salons and dinners most weeks.
Sundai.club is the largest AI hacker community born out of Harvard and MIT, with more than 130 hackathons shipped back-to-back over the last 2.5 years — one every Sunday without stopping. 1000+ projects, many funded by VCs, YC and others.
RSIhouse.ai is a weekly open neutral space for hacks and dinners dedicated to recursive self-improvement. We cover post-training, evals, harness engineering, self-play and swarm intelligence. Every week we explore the limits of RSI.
Autolab.ai is building infrastructure for RSI. Starting with evals, Autolab enables fully autonomous continual learning and ownership of your own enterprise AI models that get better with every API call you make.
Superradiant is a research lab building self-improving agents, bringing the rapid advances in mathematics to the sciences. The name comes from superradiance, the quantum effect where emitters that fall into phase radiate together and the light grows with N² instead of N. Their founders, Micah Stubbs and Alejandro Zarzuelo Urdiales, put this series together.

Join us Tuesday, November 10th at 5:30 PM for a talk with Andrew Hogan, Head of Insights at Figma. Drawing on years of research at Figma and his time as an analyst at Forrester, Andrew studies how design is changing in an era where AI, new tools, and new roles are reshaping how digital products get made. His work focuses on the real behavior inside teams: who is actually doing design, how decisions get made, and what separates the organizations that ship consistently great experiences from everyone else.
In his talk, The New Rules of Design, Andrew will present empirical findings on the changing role of designers and the increasing participation of "designers by another name" across product, engineering, marketing, and other functions. He will examine how AI-generated interfaces and accelerated prototyping are reshaping design practice, and identify domains where distinctly human judgment, interpretation, and taste remain central. Moving from popular discourse to research-backed insights, he will articulate emerging principles for contemporary design work, including cross-disciplinary collaboration, pathways for junior practitioners in a senior-leaning labor market, and strategies for sustaining a distinctive design language in a world where interface creation is widely accessible.This event is free and open to the public.....................​Design Field Notes is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff at jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

App stores are crowded, paid acquisition keeps getting more expensive, and more people now ask AI tools what to download, buy or try before they ever reach your store page or website. Each new user costs more than the last. So the growth question is changing: it is less about getting more users and more about finding the right ones and keeping them.
This evening is a small, off-the-record conversation among marketing, growth and product leaders at consumer apps, brands and game studios about what happens after the install. No slides, no presentations, no vendor pitches. Just peers comparing what they are testing, what they measure and what they would not do again.

Where new users actually find consumer apps and brands now: storefronts, creators, shared links and AI answers
Where teams are moving budget as paid acquisition gets more expensive
The first session, first week and first month, and what decides whether a user stays
Spotting a change in user behavior fast enough to act on it, and what AI is changing about that
Showing a CEO or board that retention, not just installs, is driving revenue

CMOs and VPs of Marketing, Heads of Growth and Product Growth leaders, Lifecycle and Retention leaders, and Data and Analytics leaders at Bay Area consumer apps, marketplaces, games and consumer brands.

Wednesday we're hosting a Lightning Mesh hack night @ Embassy -- home of the first Lightning Mesh permanent installation. We'll be looking at the local-first distributed service mesh, and possibly hacking together a LoRA integration with our resilient WiFi mesh system.
Come & make your project, build DWeb tech together, explore resilient communication patterns, local-first software stacks, and play around with technology.
We will see about storing sensitive data locally (like room recordings), and make democratic house decisions over how that data is used (feeding it to local transcription models, what LLMs can be used for analysis, etc).  Knowledge of Iroh and/or babeld routing is a plus. All levels of technical proficiency are welcome.
Lightning Mesh is a project begun out of the needs of refugees and political dissidents in oppressive regimes, that became a technical proof-of-concept, addressing how centralized authority presents single-point-of-failure chokepoints which can be used against people, and engineering those out of our networking stacks. Amid a growing sense that connectivity could and should be a commons, Lightning Mesh is an attempt to engineer a different way, applying the techniques of decentralized and distributed systems to serve actual people, add censorship-resistant communication to off-the-shelf routers, and create a basis for a distributed local-first service mesh not dependent on ISP-granted internet.

🧠 What if people with paralysis could move again?
Roughly one in fifty Americans lives with some form of paralysis, most often caused by stroke or spinal cord injury. In these cases, the pathway between brain and body has been interrupted, but the neural signals that would normally drive movement are still very much alive at the source.
Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a way around the injury. By reading signals directly from the brain and rerouting them to a device, whether a robotic arm, a computer cursor, or the person's own paralyzed limb, this technology can restore a kind of movement that was once thought to be lost.
Join Kushaal Rao, a PhD candidate in neuroscience at Brown University, as he demystifies how brain-computer interfaces actually work, where the science currently stands, and what the future might hold for people living with paralysis. ✨

Join Crosstown Trails founder Bob Siegel on a 6-mile walk from Lands End to Presidio Tunnel Tops. Our route follows Section 5 of the new Roundabout as well as a stretch of the new Golden Gate Dozen Trail. At Land’s End, we’ll take in the views and imagine what life might have been like long ago – in the early 20th century when the Sutro Baths were in their heyday, or even farther back, when Yelamu Ohlone lived off the land. We’ll head east along the scenic Coastal Trail, following the old rail line that once brought visitors to Adolph Sutro’s oceanside attractions. We weave through the beautiful Sea Cliff neighborhood, hit the sand at famed Baker Beach, and climb the notorious Sand Ladder. We’ll be rewarded by breathtaking views of the Marin Headlands on our way to the Golden Gate Bridge. We descend to Crissy Field, a historic 1920s airfield, and finish at the main post of the Presidio, which is celebrating its 250th anniversary.
While the walk is entirely free, your optional donations to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy as well as the Crosstown Trails directly fund the upkeep of these stunning public spaces. Come discover how truly connected our city’s parks and neighborhoods really are.
Route Overview
The 6-mile point-to-point walk hugs San Francisco's dramatic northwestern edge. You can visit The Roundabout for self-guided exploration of the full 38-mile trail any time of the year.
Travel & Logistics
Because this is a point-to-point walk, we recommend taking public transit.
Getting to the start: Meet at Lands End Lookout Visitor Center, convenient to the Muni 38R Geary Rapid and the Muni 18 46th Ave.
Returning from the finish: The walk ends at Presidio Tunnel Tops, a major transit hub. Catch the free Presidio GO Shuttle, the Muni 43 Masonic, or the Muni 30 Stockton, all near the park's many dining options.
The fine print: Terrain is a mix of dirt trails, sand, pavement, and stairs. Bring snacks, water, layers, and anything else you need.
Co-hosted by SF Crosstown Trails and the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy

Dosu - The first agent productivity platform. It automatically identifies recurring friction across coding agent sessions, teaches agents how to overcome it, and improves the code, config, or tooling in their environment to fix the underlying issues. The result is more autonomous agents, fewer wasted tokens, and less work for developers to review and correct.
Hotdata is instant data infrastructure for AI agents. Let every agent spin up on-demand low latency databases to search, query, and analyze data concurrently. Built in Rust on Apache DataFusion and DuckLake, Hotdata lets developers spin up isolated databases on demand without provisioning or managing database infrastructure.

What does it actually take to get a robot out of the lab and into the real world? Three founders who have done it in three very different ways sit down for an honest panel at Mission Robotics.
Thursday, Nov 12, 5 to 8 pm at Mission Robotics, 3001 19th St, San Francisco
THE PANEL
Anand Lalwani, Co-founder, Cardinal Robotics (Forbes 30 Under 30)Anand worked as a janitor before earning his robotics PhD at Stanford. He started Cardinal as a student, and it has grown to 30,000+ cleaning robots deployed with partners, without institutional venture money. On the panel: what running robots at scale teaches you that a demo never will.
Vatan Aksoy Tezer, Co-founder & CEO, Neuromorphic (YC S26)Vatan is a maintainer of MoveIt, the open source software behind countless robot arms, and spent the last four years building robots in Tokyo and Singapore. Neuromorphic gives any robot body a brain, starting with robots that run experiments in real wet labs. On the panel: building robot software that works on any hardware.
Max Williams, Co-founder & CEO, Axonnic (YC F26)Max did his research at Oxford on reading the muscle signals in your forearm. Axonnic turns that into a sleeve that captures how skilled hands move and how hard they press, so robots can learn dexterous work. On the panel: why video alone won't teach robots to use their hands.
WHAT WE'LL DIG INTO
What breaks when a robot leaves the lab, and what you only learn from customers
Where the data to train robots really comes from
When to build, buy or rent out your robots
What each of them would do differently if they started again

Join us for a hands-on workshop on model customization with AWS and NVIDIA.
As companies move from AI prototypes to production, off-the-shelf models may not meet the accuracy, latency, and cost requirements. Whether it's an agent that drops tools, a chatbot that hallucinates, the model needs to learn your data, your rules, your domain. Fine-tuning a smaller open-weight model like Nemotron 3 on targeted tasks can match or exceed much larger proprietary models, delivering real cost savings while keeping your data inside your own secure infrastructure.
This workshop gives you the hands-on experience to make that happen, and you'll leave with a customized model and a follow-up plan in hand.
What You'll Learn:
Apply a customization framework to decide when to prompt-engineer vs. fine-tune
Run a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) job on Nemotron 3 using Amazon Sagemaker AI
Learn how model customization can improve agentic systems
Understand when and how to use different types of fine-tuning techniques
Evaluate your customized model against your baseline using custom metrics and benchmark evaluations
Deploy your fine-tuned model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint

Guy Farber, Global Head of GTM at NVIDIA

event.description:
Worlds for Agents: World Models and the Agents That Learn Inside Them
A Frontier Research Club session hosted at SignalFire.
If a model can generate a world, an agent can practice in it. This session asks how far that loop actually goes.
World models promise to make agent training cheap: generate a world, let an agent act in it, score the attempt, repeat. In late 2025, DeepMind's SIMA 2 agent kept improving inside worlds generated by Genie 3, with no new human demonstrations. Whether this scales comes down to two open questions: can a generated world hold together for longer than a few minutes, and do skills learned inside one carry over to the real world?
Bonnie Li is a Research Scientist at OpenAI. At Google DeepMind, she worked on Gemini, the Genie world models and SIMA 2, and she began her research career at Mila with Yoshua Bengio.
Pre-reads go to confirmed guests the week before. Come having read them; the discussion starts at depth.
The Frontier Research Club is a curated forum for rigorous, technical discussion at the frontier of AI. We convene researchers from the frontier labs, Stanford, Berkeley and leading startups to examine concrete work (papers, methods and results) with a bias toward assumptions, evaluation methodology, failure modes, and what would count as convincing evidence.
Each session features 2 talks selected for rigor and discussion value. Presentations are intentionally brief so the majority of time is reserved for questions and critique. Papers and supporting materials are shared in advance to ensure a high-baseline conversation.

Bonnie will walk through what it takes for a world model to be something an agent can learn in, not just watch: worlds that stay consistent as the agent acts, respond to what it does, and come with tasks and rewards generated alongside them. She'll close on the failure modes that matter for training, including agents that learn to exploit the simulator's errors instead of the skill.

event.description:
This week's reading:
Neural Networks Are Already Clean (Nick Cammarata, Goodfire)
Link: https://already-clean.goodfire.com/
About the session:
A common view in interpretability is that neural networks are tangled knots: individual neurons do several unrelated jobs (polysemanticity), because networks cram more concepts than they have room for into shared neurons (superposition). If that is right, you cannot study neurons directly and need tools like sparse autoencoders to unfold the network first.
This essay argues the opposite. It revisits classic examples such as the InceptionV1 "cat and car" neuron and re-reads them as ordinary features like V-shape and pose detectors. It then looks at vision models of very different sizes and at language-model neurons in Qwen3-32B. The author's claim is that most apparent polysemanticity comes from fixable causes (weak visualization tools, missing architecture features, thin datasets) and from neurons growing in several directions over training, not from superposition.
Thomas will walk through the post, then step back and cover some wider AI interpretability concepts at a high level, so you do not need a background in the field.
Relevant to anyone curious about how models work inside, from newcomers to interpretability to people who have used SAEs. No preparation required. Come read and discuss with us.
Thomas will lead the discussion this week.

Build a Sovereign AI Model Factory: an ML Engineer Agent that evaluates, fine-tunes, deploys, and improves open models using Union on your cloud.
The best AI teams aren't renting every capability from an external API, they're building systems they own and control. In this hands-on session at the AWS Loft, we'll build exactly that.
We'll start with a walkthrough where we build a LangGraph-powered agent that evaluates open models in parallel, fine-tunes promising candidates, deploys the winner, and retrains automatically when performance drops. Think of it as the first brick in your own model factory: a repeatable system for evaluating, improving, and deploying models you control, not a black box you call and hope for the best.
Along the way, you'll see how Union.ai gives your workflows a durable runtime with infrastructure as context, so agents adapt infra resources, recover from failures, and keep moving without re-running completed work. And because it all runs in your own AWS account, you own the full stack end to end: your models, your data, your infrastructure, your IP.
Then we switch into hack night mode: keep building on the example, bring your own models or datasets, experiment with evals and fine-tuning, extend open models to different parts of your agent, or start something new around the same ideas.
For teams thinking about sovereign AI, this is a practical starting point for owning more of your stack, the weights, the training loop, the evals, and the infrastructure it runs on, all on AWS.
Bring a laptop. Leave with a factory.All guests must be 18+ and present a valid government-issued physical photo ID at check-in (digital IDs are not accepted). Scooters and bikes are not permitted in any Amazon building, and there is no on-site parking.

event.description:
How does a model's understanding of the physical world translate into reliable manipulation? Learning to predict what happens next and learning to act both depend on the training data, representations, and feedback available to the system.
The second Robot Learning meetup brings together builders working on world models, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and dexterous manipulation. Hosted by HackerSquad and presented by Bright Data, the evening puts data at the center of the conversation: what models can learn from video and demonstrations, how that learning connects to control, and how teams evaluate progress.
We'll start with a few short demos, hear from practitioners in a panel discussion, and leave plenty of time to meet other robotics and physical AI teams.
What we'll explore
World representations, prediction, and their relationship to planning and action.
Learning manipulation from demonstrations and other visual data, including the limits of transfer to a physical task.
Building useful training and evaluation datasets, understanding failure cases, and improving robustness.
Who this is for
Robotics founders, researchers, ML engineers, and builders working on world models, VLAs, manipulation, and training data for physical AI. Bring a research question, a data bottleneck, or lessons from a system you are building.
Schedule
All times are Pacific Time (America/Los_Angeles).
5:00 PM — Doors Open: Check in, meet fellow builders, and settle in.
5:45 PM — Programming Begins: A few short demos, with builders showing their work and sharing the data and engineering decisions behind it.
6:15 PM — Panel Discussion: A conversation with practitioners about the evening's topic, followed by audience questions.
7:00 PM — Networking: Continue the conversation with founders, engineers, researchers, and the teams behind the demos.
8:30 PM — Doors Close.
Location and registration
Join us at Bright Data — Web Data Loft, 625 2nd St, San Francisco, CA 94107. Hosted by HackerSquad and presented by Bright Data.
Attendance is free, with registration subject to approval. Demo teams and panelists will be announced.
